title: Tyrian purple from murex snails and William Perkin's mauve (1856)

sources.publisher: Marine Science Institute, The University of Texas at Austin (Science and the Sea)
sources.title: Royal Colors

sources.publisher: Fashion Institute of Technology, Fashion History Timeline
sources.title: Aniline dyes

facts.text: Tyrian purple was named for the city of Tyre in ancient Phoenicia, where much of it was made.
Purple and related dyes were produced as early as about 4,000 years ago and were worn by the rich in Phoenicia, Greece and Rome; purple became a symbol of royalty.
The dye came from murex sea snails, whose glands produce a mucus that knocks out prey and wards off predators.
Making the dye involved leaving thousands of snails to dry in the sun, boiling them and removing the glands, a smelly process.
A huge number of snails was needed for a small amount of dye, so it was expensive, could be worth more than gold, and was reserved for royalty and the very rich.
People not of the right class who were caught wearing the color could be severely punished, even executed.
In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old student at the Royal College of Chemistry in London, was trying to make the anti-malaria drug quinine.
Instead of the white crystals he hoped for, Perkin obtained a dark, sticky mass; hot alcohol dissolved part of it into a violet liquid that could dye silk and wool.
Perkin patented the dye, which became known as aniline violet or mauveine (mauve); it is often called the first synthetic dye and was made from coal tar.
The new aniline dye was cost-effective to produce and resisted fading.
In August 1859 the satirical magazine Punch described the craze for purple as mauve measles.
Other synthetic dyes followed in shades such as magenta, green, yellow, red and blue, and by about 1860 aniline dyes were widely available.
Cheap synthetic purple changed the social meaning of the color, which lost its association with royalty.
